opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think handcrafted pipelines, and tokenization is probably the most prominent example, are really a sign that we haven't quite figured out the right end-to-end approach yet. If you look at the history of deep learning, the recurring lesson is that whenever we have some handcrafted stage, like feature engineering in computer vision or hand-designed acoustic features in speech, eventually it gets absorbed into the model and learned directly from data, and things get better when that happens. That's basically the bitter lesson: methods that lean on learning and compute tend to win over methods that bake in human priors.

Tokenization is a great case study. It's a separate preprocessing step, trained with a completely different, fairly heuristic objective, and then frozen before the model ever sees the data. It has all kinds of known issues. It's brittle to spelling variations and typos, it handles numbers and arithmetic strangely, it treats different languages unevenly, and it causes odd failure modes, like models not being able to count the letters in a word. It also doesn't translate cleanly to other modalities. For audio, DNA, or raw pixels there isn't an obvious analogue of a "word," so you end up designing a new ad hoc chunking scheme for each domain.

So my view is that in the long run these pipelines should go away, or at least become much less important. Ideally the model works on raw data, like bytes or the rawest available signal, and learns its own way of grouping and abstracting information, which is where things like dynamic chunking or hierarchical architectures come in. The model should decide where the meaningful boundaries are, and those boundaries can depend on context and on the modality, rather than being fixed ahead of time by a heuristic.

That said, I'm pragmatic about it. Tokenization exists for a good reason: it compresses the sequence, which makes Transformers far more efficient, since attention scales badly with length. The handcrafted step is really compensating for an architectural limitation. That's part of why I find the architecture question so interesting. If you have models that handle long sequences efficiently and can build their own abstractions, then many of these handcrafted components stop being necessary. I don't think we're fully there yet, but I'm fairly confident that's the direction things will go.

r001.rationale: It describes handcrafted stages as signs that the right end-to-end approach has not yet been found and says they are eventually absorbed into models, even while acknowledging that tokenization serves a useful purpose.

r002.rationale: It predicts these pipelines should go away or become much less important as models learn from raw data and build their own abstractions.

r003.rationale: It advocates having the model learn meaningful groupings and boundaries from raw data, rather than relying on tokenization fixed in advance by a heuristic.

r004.rationale: It says tokenization has known problems, including brittleness to typos, uneven language handling, and odd counting failures, illustrating problems its predefined rules do not address.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think about a lot, and honestly my view is that handcrafted pipelines are kind of a transitional thing. They're useful right now, but I don't think they're where the field ends up.

The clearest example for me is tokenization. If you look at how we train language models today, there's this whole stage before the model ever sees the data where we chop text up into tokens using a heuristic like byte-pair encoding. And that works, it's gotten us really far, but it's fundamentally a handcrafted step. Someone decided on a vocabulary, someone decided on a merge procedure, and the model just has to live with that decision. It's not learned end to end. And it causes all sorts of weird artifacts, like models being bad at spelling or arithmetic or handling certain languages, because the units they're operating on were chosen by a human heuristic rather than discovered by the model.

And I'd say that's actually a pattern across deep learning. Every time there's been a handcrafted feature-engineering stage, it's eventually been absorbed into the model. Computer vision used to be all SIFT features and hand-designed descriptors, and then convolutional networks just learned better features from raw pixels. Speech used to rely heavily on MFCCs and other hand-engineered representations, and now models operate much closer to the raw waveform. So the bitter-lesson framing applies here: things we hardcode are usually things the model could learn better if we gave it the right architecture and enough compute.

The reason tokenization has stuck around, though, is that it's actually doing real work. It compresses the sequence, which matters a lot when your core primitive is attention and attention is quadratic in sequence length. So the pipeline isn't just a convenience, it's compensating for a limitation in the architecture. And that's the part I find interesting. If you want to get rid of the handcrafted stage, you can't just delete it, you have to replace it with something inside the model that does that job of compressing and finding the right level of abstraction in the data. That's a lot of why I've been interested in state space models and more recently in things like dynamic chunking, where the model learns its own segmentation of the input instead of having it imposed from outside.

So my long-term view is that these pipelines are scaffolding. They tell you something about what the model is currently missing, which is really valuable as a signal. But the goal should be to build architectures that make them unnecessary, and I think over the next few years we'll see a lot of that scaffolding come down.

r001.rationale: The response calls handcrafted pipelines transitional and scaffolding, but does not address whether they remain temporary when strong priors guide their design.

r002.rationale: It predicts that architectures will make handcrafted stages unnecessary and says this scaffolding will come down over the next few years.

r003.rationale: It advocates replacing imposed tokenization with an in-model process that learns its own segmentation.

r004.rationale: It describes artifacts such as spelling, arithmetic, and language difficulties arising from human-chosen tokenization rules.

astra-6.text:
I tend to think of handcrafted pipelines as useful, but probably not the long-term approach. When you build a pipeline with a lot of separate processing stages, you’re making assumptions about what information matters and how the model should use it. Those assumptions can help, especially when data or compute is limited, but they can also constrain what the model can learn.

One of the broader trends in deep learning is moving more of that processing into the model itself. So the question I’m interested in is: can we build architectures that learn directly from less-processed data, efficiently enough that we don’t need all those handcrafted stages? You still need some inductive bias, but ideally it gives the model a useful structure without prescribing the entire solution.

r001.rationale: The response says pipelines are probably not the long-term approach and discusses inductive bias, but it does not clearly characterize them as temporary even when strong priors guide their design.

r002.rationale: It describes moving more processing into the model and asks whether architectures can learn from less-processed data without handcrafted stages.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention tokenization or advocate learning it end to end instead of using a predefined scheme.

r004.rationale: It says pipeline assumptions can constrain learning, but does not claim that their rules inevitably encounter problems they do not address.

sol-6.1.text:
I tend to think of handcrafted data-processing pipelines as a useful starting point, but I’m skeptical of them as the long-term solution. You’re baking in assumptions about what information matters and how the model should use it. Those assumptions can help, especially when data or compute is limited, but they can also become a bottleneck.

One of the recurring themes in deep learning is that, as we get better models and more resources, we can learn more of that processing directly from the data. So the direction I’m interested in is making models that can handle more of the underlying input themselves. That doesn’t mean removing every inductive bias—you still need to choose an architecture—but ideally you’re giving the model a useful structure without prescribing every step of the computation.

r001.rationale: The response calls pipelines a useful starting point and questions them as a long-term solution, but does not say this holds even when strong priors guide their design.

r002.rationale: It favors learning more processing from data, but does not predict eliminating hard-coded data processing.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention tokenization or replacing a predefined tokenization scheme with learned tokenization.

r004.rationale: It says pipelines can become a bottleneck, but does not claim their rules inevitably fail to address some problems.
